Stage 3 · Language

Saying sorry, and answering it

Two sets of phrases, three levels of formality, and one word to avoid entirely.

Read these two apologies.
  • I’m sorry if you were offended but you started it.
  • I’m sorry. It was my fault. I should never have said it.
Why does the first one not work as an apology?
‘Sorry’ on its own only signals that you noticed.

A real apology in English does more than express regret. It names what you did, accepts responsibility for it, and says what will happen next. An apology that stops at sorry leaves the other person still holding the problem, and in professional contexts it is often read as evasive rather than as brief.

The full sequence has five moves: the apology itself; a statement of what you did; an acceptance of responsibility (It was my fault, I should never have…); an explanation; and a commitment about the future (It won’t happen again). The should have structure from the previous lesson does the third move, which is why the two lessons sit together.

The explanation is the dangerous one. It must be short — one clause — and it must not become a defence. I’ve had some family issues this month, but that’s no excuse works because it explains and then closes the subject. A long explanation reads as self-justification and cancels out the apology that preceded it. A useful test: if your explanation is longer than your apology, rewrite it.

Two formal points are worth settling in advance because learners get them wrong consistently. Sorry for takes an -ing form (sorry for being late) while sorry about takes a noun (sorry about the delay). And apologise is intransitive: you apologise to a person for a thing, never I apologise you.

Before you look at the table: the tables below give the apology moves in order and then the response phrases. Watch the prepositions in the first table — for and about are not interchangeable.
Apologizing — from casual to formal
LevelPhraseWhere
casualSorry about that. · Sorry for being late.friends, quick messages
normalI’m really sorry about… · It was my fault.colleagues, most situations
strongerI should never have… · That was careless of me.when it actually mattered
formalI’d like to apologize for… · Please accept my apologies.writing, work, customers
promisingIt won’t happen again. · I’ll make sure…the end of an apology
Answering an apology — from casual to formal
LevelPhrase
casualDon’t worry about it. · No harm done. · That’s all right.
normalDon’t worry, these things happen. · It’s not a problem.
honestThank you for saying so. · I appreciate that.
formalThank you for letting me know. · That’s very good of you.

The grammar of the two verbs. Sorry for / about + a noun or -ing: Sorry for being late. Apologize for + a noun or -ing: I apologize for the delay. Never I apologize you.

Do not say but. Everything after it cancels everything before it. If there is a reason, give it as information, not as a defence — and give it after the apology, never inside it.

Sorry if is not an apology. I’m sorry if you were upset says you may not have done anything wrong. I’m sorry that you had to read it accepts that they were.

Name the specific thing. Sorry about yesterday is weaker than Sorry I copied in the whole team. The more precise the apology, the more it sounds like you understood what you did.

Now say it. Apologize for the same thing three times, at three levels.

Full grammar reference — apologising, and responding to an apology

What it is

The functional language of repair. A full apology in English has up to five parts: the apology itself, an acknowledgement of what you did, an acceptance of responsibility, an explanation without excuse, and a commitment about the future. The response set is smaller but equally fixed: accepting, minimising, and reassuring.

What it means, and what it does

Sorry on its own signals only that you noticed. A working apology names the harm (I know this put you in a difficult position), accepts responsibility (It was my fault), and promises change (It won’t happen again). The grammar of the lesson — should have, sorry for + -ing, apologise for + noun — exists to make those moves possible.

When and why we use it

A real apology in English does more than express regret. It names what you did, accepts responsibility for it, and says what will happen next. An apology that stops at sorry leaves the other person still holding the problem, and in professional contexts it is often read as evasive rather than as brief.

The full sequence has five moves: the apology itself; a statement of what you did; an acceptance of responsibility (It was my fault, I should never have…); an explanation; and a commitment about the future (It won’t happen again). The should have structure from the previous lesson does the third move, which is why the two lessons sit together.

The explanation is the dangerous one. It must be short — one clause — and it must not become a defence. I’ve had some family issues this month, but that’s no excuse works because it explains and then closes the subject. A long explanation reads as self-justification and cancels out the apology that preceded it. A useful test: if your explanation is longer than your apology, rewrite it.

Two formal points are worth settling in advance because learners get them wrong consistently. Sorry for takes an -ing form (sorry for being late) while sorry about takes a noun (sorry about the delay). And apologise is intransitive: you apologise to a person for a thing, never I apologise you.

Typical situations

You need this for missing a deadline, arriving late, forgetting something, causing somebody extra work, and for responding when somebody apologises to you — where English strongly prefers to minimise (Don’t worry, these things happen).

  • Apologising informally — the everyday spoken form.I’m really sorry about yesterday.
  • Apologising formally — in writing, or when the matter is serious.Please accept my apologies for the late submission.
  • Naming what you did — sorry for + -ing.I’m sorry for missing the deadline without warning you.
  • Accepting responsibility — the move that most learners omit.It was my fault. I should never have left it so late.
  • Explaining without excusing — one clause, then back to the apology.I’ve had some family issues this month, but that’s no excuse.
  • Committing to change — the forward-looking move.It won’t happen again. I’ll make sure the next one is on time.
  • Accepting an apology — the standard replies.Don’t worry, these things happen. · No harm done.
  • Minimising politely — when you want to close the subject.It’s fine, really. · Please don’t worry about it.

How it differs from similar structures

Sorry (something went wrong) · Excuse me (before you interrupt or ask) · Pardon? / Sorry? (I didn’t hear). Three different jobs that learners often merge into one.
I’m sorry (informal, spoken, personal) · I apologise for… (neutral–formal) · Please accept my apologies for… (formal, written). Choose by how serious the matter is and who you are writing to.

How to build it

Informal: I’m (really / so) sorry about + noun  ·  I’m sorry for + verb-ing
Formal: Please accept my apologies for + noun / verb-ing  ·  I would like to apologise for + noun
Responsibility: It was my fault.  ·  I should(n’t) have + past participle
Commitment: It won’t happen again.  ·  I’ll make sure + clause
Apologising — aboutI’m sorry about the delay. — about + noun
Apologising — forI’m sorry for replying so late. — for + -ing
Apologising — thatI’m sorry that I didn’t tell you sooner.
Verb formapologise (BrE) / apologize (AmE): I apologise for the inconvenience.
Noun formapology / apologies: Please accept my apologies.
ResponsibilityIt was my fault. · I take full responsibility. · I should never have…
CommitmentIt won’t happen again. · I’ll make sure it doesn’t happen again.
AcceptingDon’t worry, these things happen. · No harm done. · That’s all right.

Spelling and word order

  • British English writes apologise and apologising; American English writes apologize. Both are correct — be consistent within one text.
  • The noun is apology (plural apologies); the verb is apologise. I apology and my apologise are both errors.

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • sorry is stressed on the first syllable: SOR-ry. Apologise is stressed on the second: a-POL-o-gise. The noun apology keeps the same stress: a-POL-o-gy.
  • A falling tone on sorry sounds sincere; a rising tone can sound like a question or, in British English, like pardon?
  • should’ve and shouldn’t’ve appear constantly in apologies — see the pronunciation note in Lesson 32.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Sorry for takes -ing; sorry about takes a noun. Sorry for being late and sorry about the delay are both correct; sorry for be late and sorry about being the delay are not.
  • Apologise is intransitive: you apologise to a person for a thing. I apologise you is wrong; say I apologise to you for…
  • An explanation is not an excuse. Give it in one clause and return to the apology; a long explanation reads as self-defence and undoes the apology.
  • Excuse me is not an apology. It is used before you interrupt or pass someone; sorry is used after something has gone wrong.
  • Match the register to the harm. Please accept my apologies in a text message to a friend sounds cold; Sorry about that! in a formal complaint response sounds careless.
  • In responses, English strongly prefers to minimise: Don’t worry, No harm done, These things happen. Simply saying I accept your apology sounds severe.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I apologise you for the delay. → I apologise for the delay. / I apologise to you for the delay.Apologise takes to before the person and for before the thing.
  • Sorry for be late. → Sorry for being late.Sorry for takes the -ing form.
  • Please accept my apologise. → Please accept my apologies.Apologies is the noun; apologise is the verb.
  • Excuse me for missing the deadline. → I’m sorry for missing the deadline.Excuse me comes before an interruption, not after a mistake.
  • I should never sent that message. → I should never have sent that message.Should have + past participle.
  • Sorry about I was late. → Sorry I was late. / Sorry about being late.About takes a noun or -ing, not a clause.

More examples in context

  • informalI’m really sorry about the mess — I’ll clear it up now.
  • naming the actionI’m sorry for not telling you sooner.
  • formal writtenPlease accept my apologies for the late submission of this term’s work.
  • responsibilityIt was entirely my fault. I should have checked the date.
  • emphatic regretI should never have sent that message without reading it again.
  • explanation, not excuseI’ve had some family issues this month, but that’s no excuse.
  • commitmentIt won’t happen again — I’ll set a reminder next time.
  • asking for an extensionI’d be grateful if you could give me until Friday.
  • acceptingDon’t worry, these things happen.
  • minimisingNo harm done — please don’t give it another thought.

A tip for remembering it

Write every apology in five short moves, in this order: 1 say sorry, 2 name exactly what you did, 3 take responsibility (It was my fault / I should have…), 4 explain in one clause only, 5 say what you will do next time. If your explanation is longer than your apology, rewrite it.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Sorry for + -ing; sorry about + noun.
  2. Apologise to a person for a thing; the noun is apology / apologies.
  3. Take responsibility explicitly — It was my fault, I should have…
  4. Keep the explanation to one clause; it is not an excuse.
  5. End with a commitment: It won’t happen again.
  6. Accept an apology by minimising: Don’t worry, these things happen.

Stage 5 · Main input

A message of apology

Read it as a writer. You are going to write one like it.

Before you read: what does a real apology have that a bad one does not?

Choose one. The model does three of these and never asks for the fourth.

Subject: About yesterday’s email

Dear Aigerim,

I’d like to apologize for the email I sent to the whole team yesterday afternoon.

It was my fault. I read your message about the deadline, I was tired and passionate about the project, and I replied in about ninety seconds. I should never have copied in the whole team, and I certainly shouldn’t have written that the timeline was somebody else’s fantasy. If I had waited until this morning, I would have said none of it.

I’m sorry — not because the email made me look bad, but because you had to read it in front of eleven colleagues. That was careless of me and it was unfair on you.

I’ve written to the team this morning to say that the criticism was mine and that it was wrongly directed. If there is anything else you would like me to do, please tell me and I’ll do it.

Please accept my apologies. It won’t happen again: I’ve set myself a rule that stops me from sending anything the same day I write it, if I write it angry.

Best wishes,
Timur

What the model does, in five moves
  • Apologizes in the first line, before any explanation. The reader knows immediately what this is.
  • Names the exact things — copying in the team, and one specific sentence. Not “my tone”.
  • Gives the reason without but. Tired, and ninety seconds. Stated as fact, not as a defence.
  • Says why he is sorry — the harm to her, not the damage to himself.
  • Reports what he has already done, then promises. In that order. And it never asks to be forgiven.
  • Then write your own message of apology (80–140 words) using the same five moves, and check that your explanation is shorter than your apology.
